items.title: An open world model for human health and mortality

fields.title: An open world model for human health and mortality
fields.description: Aging shows itself in whole organisms, in populations and in the lifespan of a species, while most AI for biology works on proteins and cells. The talk covers AI models of aging at six scales: species, population, individual, tissue, cell and molecule.

items.title: Massive AI agent mining of aging-modifying interventions from millions of molecular profiles

fields.title: Massive AI agent mining of aging-modifying interventions from millions of molecular profiles

aboutWork.text: Decades of publicly available molecular studies have generated millions of samples testing diverse interventions, yet these datasets were rarely analyzed for their effects on aging. Aging clocks now enable biological age estimation and life outcome prediction from molecular data, creating an opportunity to systematically mine this untapped resource. We developed ClockBase Agent, a publicly accessible platform that reanalyzes millions of human and mouse methylation and RNA-seq samples by integrating them with over 40 aging clock predictions. ClockBase Agent employs specialized AI agents that autonomously generate aging-focused hypotheses, evaluate intervention effects on biological age, conduct literature reviews, and produce scientific reports across all datasets.
aboutWork.title: Autonomous AI Agents Discover Aging Interventions from Millions of Molecular Profiles

fields.description: ClockBase Agent uses AI agents to reanalyze millions of public human and mouse methylation and RNA-seq samples with more than 40 aging clocks. Across 43,602 intervention-control comparisons it found more than 500 interventions associated with lower biological age. One candidate, ouabain, slowed frailty progression and reduced neuroinflammation in aged mice.

items.title: Decoding the Aging Methylome: From Causal Inference to Foundation Models

fields.title: Decoding the Aging Methylome: From Causal Inference to Foundation Models
fields.abstract: In this talk, Kejun Ying will first present how integrating GWAS and Mendelian randomization with methylation data leads to causality-enriched aging clocks that separate detrimental from adaptive changes. He will then introduce MethylGPT, a transformer-based foundation model trained on over 150,000 methylation profiles across diverse populations. The model demonstrates state-of-the-art methylation prediction (R=0.929) and maintains robust performance with up to 70% missing data.

items.title: MethylGPT: A Foundation Model for the DNA Methylome

fields.title: MethylGPT: A Foundation Model for the DNA Methylome
fields.event: Keystone Symposia: Aging: New Frontiers in Rejuvenation and Gerotherapeutics

relatedWork.title: MethylGPT: A Foundation Model for the DNA Methylome

aboutWork.text: DNA methylation serves as a powerful biomarker for disease diagnosis and biological age assessment. However, current analytical approaches often rely on linear models that cannot capture the complex, context-dependent nature of methylation regulation. Here we present MethylGPT, a transformer-based foundation model trained on 226,555 (154,063 after QC and deduplication) human methylation profiles spanning diverse tissue types from 5,281 datasets, curated 49,156 CpG sites, and 7.6 billion training tokens. MethylGPT learns biologically meaningful representations of CpG sites, capturing both local genomic context and higher-order chromosomal features without external supervision.

items.title: Epigenetic Clocks and Mendelian Randomization

fields.title: Epigenetic Clocks and Mendelian Randomization

aboutWork.text: Machine learning models based on DNA methylation data can predict biological age but often lack causal insights. By harnessing large-scale genetic data through epigenome-wide Mendelian randomization, we identified CpG sites potentially causal for aging-related traits. Neither the existing epigenetic clocks nor age-related differential DNA methylation are enriched in these sites. These CpGs include sites that contribute to aging and protect against it, yet their combined contribution negatively affects age-related traits.

fields.abstract: Machine learning models that use DNA markers can estimate the age of biological samples. However, understanding why these markers change with age is challenging because it's hard to prove that these changes cause aging-related traits. items.title: Causal Epigenetic Age Uncouples Damage and Adaptation

fields.title: Causal Epigenetic Age Uncouples Damage and Adaptation
fields.event: 10th Aging Research and Drug Discovery conference (ARDD2023)

relatedWork.title: Causality-Enriched Epigenetic Age Uncouples Damage and Adaptation

fields.abstract: We performed epigenome-wide Mendelian Randomization using large-scale genetic data to identify CpG sites causally related to aging traits. Our findings suggest that neither existing epigenetic clocks nor age-related differential DNA methylation are enriched in putative causal CpG sites. We introduced DamAge and AdaptAge, measures of age-related damaging and adaptive changes respectively. DamAge acceleration correlates with adverse conditions, including mortality risk, while AdaptAge acceleration is linked to beneficial adaptations. Only DamAge is reversed upon cellular reprogramming. Our work provides a detailed map of CpG sites causally linked to lifespan and healthspan, enabling the development of causal biomarkers for aging and rejuvenation, and evaluation of longevity interventions.

items.title: Causal Epigenetic Age Uncouples Damage and Adaptation

fields.title: Causal Epigenetic Age Uncouples Damage and Adaptation

relatedWork.title: Causality-Enriched Epigenetic Age Uncouples Damage and Adaptation

aboutWork.text: Machine learning models based on DNA methylation can be used to predict the age of biological samples, but their interpretability is limited due to the lack of causal inferences. Here, we leveraged large-scale genetic data and performed epigenome-wide Mendelian Randomization to identify CpG sites causal to aging-related traits. We show that neither the existing epigenetic clocks nor DNA methylation changes are enriched in causal CpG sites. Causal CpGs include similar numbers of sites that contribute to aging and protect against it, yet their combined contribution negatively affects age-related traits. We developed a framework for integrating causal knowledge into epigenetic clock models and constructed DamAge and AdaptAge that measure age-related damaging and adaptive changes, respectively. DamAge acceleration is associated with various adverse conditions (e.g., mortality risk), whereas AdaptAge acceleration is related to beneficial adaptations. Only DamAge is reversed upon cell reprogramming. Our results offer a comprehensive map of CpG sites causal to lifespan and healthspan, allowing to build causal biomarkers of aging and rejuvenation and assess longevity interventions, age reversal, and aging-accelerating events.

items.title: Causal Epigenetic Age Uncouples Damage and Adaptation

fields.title: Causal Epigenetic Age Uncouples Damage and Adaptation

relatedWork.title: Causality-Enriched Epigenetic Age Uncouples Damage and Adaptation

fields.abstract: DNA methylation-based machine learning models (known as epigenetic clocks) can be used to predict the age of biological samples. Yet, it is unclear whether the clock CpG sites are causal to aging-related phenotypes. Here, we leveraged large-scale genetic data and performed epigenome-wide Mendelian Randomization to identify CpG sites causal to diverse aging-related traits. We show that neither the existing epigenetic clocks nor DNA methylation changes in general are enriched with causal CpG sites. Causal CpGs include an approximately equal number of sites that contribute to aging and protect against it, although their combined contribution negatively affects age-related traits. We constructed a causality-informed aging clock as well as clocks that measure damaging and adaptive changes, which exhibited distinct properties compared to existing clocks. Together, our results offer a comprehensive map of CpG sites causal to lifespan and healthspan, which can be used to build causal biomarkers of aging and assess longevity interventions, age reversal and aging-accelerating events.

items.title: Genetic and phenotypic evidence for causal relationships between aging and COVID-19

fields.title: Genetic and phenotypic evidence for causal relationships between aging and COVID-19
fields.abstract: Epidemiological studies revealed that the elderly and those with comorbidities are most susceptible to COVID-19. To understand how genetics affects the risk of COVID-19, we conducted a multi-instrument Mendelian Randomization (MR) analysis and found that the genetic variation that supports a longer life is significantly associated with the lower risk of COVID-19 infection, as well as being hospitalized after infected. The odds ratio is 0.31 (P = 9.7e-6) and 0.46 (P = 3.3e-4), respectively, per additional 10 years of life. We further applied aging clock models and detected an association between biological age acceleration and future incidence and severity of COVID-19 infection for all subjects and individuals free of chronic disease.

items.title: Genetic Variation, Aging & Relationship to COVID-19 | Joris Deelen, Albert Ying

fields.title: Genetic Variation, Aging & Relationship to COVID-19 | Joris Deelen, Albert Ying
fields.abstract: Epidemiological studies have revealed that the elderly and those with co-morbidities are most susceptible to COVID-19. However, the evidence of any causal link between aging and COVID-19 susceptibility is still missing. In our recent study, we conducted a multi-instrument Mendelian randomization analysis and found that the genetic variation that leads to a longer lifespan is significantly associated with a lower risk of COVID-19 infection. To examine the relationship at the phenotypic level, we applied various biological aging clock models and detected an association between the biological age acceleration and future incidence and severity of COVID-19 infection. Our findings suggest a causal relationship between aging and COVID-19, which directly point to the possibility of using anti-aging drugs to protect against COVID-19.
